text: How the task-management API uses a local Keycloak broker with Cloud-IAM as the external identity provider
textPreview: How the task-management API uses a local Keycloak broker with Cloud-IAM as the external identity provider

text: Presentation goal: make the flow repeatable, testable, and easy to explain.
textPreview: Presentation goal: make the flow repeatable, testable, and easy to explain.

text:
Open by saying this is not just a Keycloak feature demo. It explains which system issues tokens, which system authenticates external users, and how the Spring Boot app validates the result.
The main distinction: Cloud-IAM authenticates, but the local Keycloak broker issues the API token.

title: The system has three moving parts

text: The system has three moving parts
textPreview: The system has three moving parts

text: Each part has one clear security responsibility.
textPreview: Each part has one clear security responsibility.

text: Resource server. It does not log users in; it validates JWT access tokens.
textPreview: Resource server. It does not log users in; it validates JWT access tokens.

text: Local Keycloak. It owns the realm trusted by the API and can redirect login to external providers.
textPreview: Local Keycloak. It owns the realm trusted by the API and can redirect login to external providers.

text: Cloud-IAM Keycloak. It authenticates the external user and sends identity claims back to the broker.
textPreview: Cloud-IAM Keycloak. It authenticates the external user and sends identity claims back to the broker.

text: The API accepts tokens from the broker only.
textPreview: The API accepts tokens from the broker only.

text: That keeps authorization centralized in the local realm even when the user originally signs in through Cloud-IAM.
textPreview: That keeps authorization centralized in the local realm even when the user originally signs in through Cloud-IAM.

text:
Explain the vocabulary first: resource server, broker, provider.
The broker is the middle Keycloak. It starts the login, delegates authentication, receives the callback, creates or links a local user, and issues the final local token.

title: Spring Boot integrates with the broker using OIDC

text: The API validates the issuer and roles from local Keycloak tokens.
textPreview: The API validates the issuer and roles from local Keycloak tokens.

text:
Every request is authenticated.
JWT roles are read from realm_access.roles.
Spring sees PORTAL_ADMIN as ROLE_PORTAL_ADMIN.
textPreview: Every request is authenticated. | JWT roles are read from realm_access.roles. | Spring sees PORTAL_ADMIN as ROLE_PORTAL_ADMIN.

text: Meaning: Cloud-IAM tokens are not accepted directly. The app trusts only tokens issued by the local broker realm.
textPreview: Meaning: Cloud-IAM tokens are not accepted directly. The app trusts only tokens issued by the local broker realm.

text:
The API is a resource server. It is not configured with Cloud-IAM as issuer. It is configured with the local Keycloak issuer.
That is why the final JWT must have iss equal to http://localhost:8081/realms/task-management-demo.

text:
Walk through this as a handshake. Cloud-IAM needs to know where to return the user. Local Keycloak needs to know Cloud-IAM's auth, token, userinfo, and JWKS endpoints.
The discovery URL fills most of the endpoint fields automatically.

text: Rule of thumb: the Spring Boot issuer-uri must match the JWT iss claim exactly.

text:
In Postman or jwt.io, decode the token and point to the iss claim. This avoids long explanations.
If the issuer does not match the Spring Boot issuer-uri, the resource server rejects the request.
